title: New Year, Qingming and the Mid-Autumn Moon
bigQuestion: How do festivals help families remember the past and show respect?

story.title: Brooms on the Hill
story.kicker: A family climbs a hill on a spring morning to care for the graves of people they love.
paragraphs: It is early April. Mei and her family drive out of the city to a quiet hillside cemetery. Her father carries a broom. Her grandmother carries a bag of oranges and a bunch of white flowers.

They stop at a stone with carved Chinese letters. This is the grave of Mei's great-grandparents. Mei never met them, but she knows their names. Her grandmother says them out loud as they begin to work.

Everyone has a job. Father sweeps away old leaves. Mei pulls weeds from the edges. Her brother wipes the stone with a wet cloth until the letters shine. Then Grandmother sets out the fruit and the flowers.

The family stands together and bows three times. Grandmother tells a story about how her father walked miles to school as a boy. Mei listens closely. On the drive home she thinks, "Now I know a little more about where I come from."
story.think: Why do you think Mei's grandmother tells stories at the grave while the family works?

sections.title: A Calendar That Follows the Moon

lessons.title: Months by the Moon
lessons.mainIdea: The traditional Chinese calendar counts months by the moon, so festival dates move on the everyday calendar.
reading: Look up at the moon for a month. It grows from a thin sliver to a full circle and back again. That trip takes about 29 and a half days. The traditional Chinese calendar uses this trip to count months.

A calendar that counts by the moon is called a *lunar calendar*. The Chinese calendar also watches the sun, so the seasons stay in place. Because it uses both, scholars call it a lunisolar calendar. Each new month starts on the night of the new moon.

Most people in China today use the same calendar as Illinois for school and work. Families use the old calendar for festivals. So Lunar New Year can fall on a different day in January or February each year.

words.d: a calendar that counts months by the changes of the moon
a special day or days that a community celebrates each year

look.title: Watch the Moon Change
look.text: Picture the sky over Chicago on four nights. Night one: no moon at all. Night eight: half a moon. Night fifteen: a round, bright full moon. Night twenty-two: half a moon again, lit on the other side.
look.prompt: On which night would a month on the Chinese calendar begin? On which night is the moon full?

check.q: What does a lunar calendar use to count months?
check.why: A lunar calendar counts months by the moon's changes, about 29 and a half days each.

check.q: Why does Lunar New Year fall on a different date each year?
choices: Families pick a new date by vote
It follows the moon, not the everyday calendar
It moves to the first snow
check.why: The festival follows the moon-based calendar, so its date moves on the everyday calendar.

check.q: When does a new month begin on the Chinese calendar?
check.why: Each month in the traditional calendar starts on the night of the new moon.

lessons.title: Twelve Animals, Twelve Years
lessons.mainIdea: Each year in the Chinese calendar has one of twelve animals, and the list repeats every twelve years.
reading: Ask a friend who celebrates Lunar New Year, "What is your animal?" They may say the Tiger or the Rabbit. Each year in the Chinese calendar is named for one of twelve animals. This set of animals is called the *zodiac*.

The twelve animals go in order: Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Goat, Monkey, Rooster, Dog and Pig. After the Pig, the list starts again with the Rat. So each animal comes back every twelve years.

A well-known folk story tells how the animals raced across a river. The order they finished became the order of the years. The clever Rat rode on the Ox's back and jumped ahead at the end. Families tell this story to children at New Year.

words.d: the set of twelve animals, one for each year, in the Chinese calendar
a story passed down by people over many years, often told out loud

look.title: The First Six Animals in Order
look.cite: Traditional order of the Chinese zodiac
look.prompt: If this year is a Dragon year, which animal comes next year?

check.q: How many animals are in the Chinese zodiac?
check.why: The zodiac has twelve animals, one for each year of a twelve-year cycle.

check.q: Which animal comes first in the cycle?
check.why: The cycle starts with the Rat and ends with the Pig.

check.q: In the folk story, how does the Rat finish first?
choices: It rides on the Ox's back and jumps ahead
check.why: The folk story says the Rat rode the Ox across the river and jumped ahead at the end.

lessons.title: The Biggest Holiday of the Year
lessons.mainIdea: Lunar New Year is a time for family meals, cleaning, red decorations and good wishes.
reading: Before Lunar New Year, many families clean their homes from top to bottom. People say this sweeps out the old year. Then they hang red paper with wishes for luck and health. Red is a color of joy in Chinese culture.

On New Year's Eve, families share a big *reunion dinner*. People travel far to be home for it. Children often get red envelopes with money inside from older relatives. Many families also honor their ancestors with food and bows.

The celebration lasts about fifteen days. It ends with the *Lantern Festival* on the first full moon of the year. Families hang lanterns and eat sweet rice balls. Round foods and a round moon stand for a family together.

words.d: the big family meal on the night before Lunar New Year
the last day of New Year, on the first full moon, with lanterns and sweet rice balls
a red paper envelope with money, given as a New Year gift

look.title: Getting Ready at Home
look.text: Picture a kitchen the day before New Year. A mother sweeps the floor. A boy tapes a red paper sign by the door. A grandfather folds dumplings on the table. A girl sets out bowls for everyone, and one extra place for an uncle arriving by train.
look.prompt: Which of these actions show caring for family? Which show getting ready for a fresh start?

check.q: What is the reunion dinner?
choices: The big family meal on New Year's Eve
A meal at the Mid-Autumn Festival
check.why: The reunion dinner is the family meal on the night before Lunar New Year.

check.q: How does the New Year season end?
choices: With the Lantern Festival on the first full moon
check.why: The Lantern Festival, on the first full moon, ends about fifteen days of New Year.

check.q: Why do many families clean before New Year?
choices: To get ready for a race
To sweep out the old year and start fresh
check.why: Families say cleaning sweeps out the old year before the new one begins.

lessons.title: Tomb-Sweeping Day
lessons.mainIdea: On Qingming, families clean the graves of their ancestors and bring gifts of food and flowers.
reading: Mei's family went to the cemetery on *Qingming*. The name means "clear and bright." It falls in early April, around April 4 or 5. In English it is often called Tomb-Sweeping Day.

On this day families visit the graves of their *ancestors*. They sweep, pull weeds and wipe the stones. Then they set out food, tea and flowers. Many bow or burn incense. Some families burn paper gifts for those who have died.

Qingming is also a spring day. Families may take walks, fly kites and enjoy the new green leaves. In Taiwan, Qingming is a public holiday. In the United States, families often visit on the weekend closest to it.

words.d: a spring festival in early April when families care for ancestors' graves; the name means clear and bright
family members who lived long ago, like great-grandparents
sticks that give off sweet-smelling smoke when burned, used to show respect

look.title: Jobs at the Grave
look.text: At the cemetery, each person has a task. One sweeps leaves. One pulls weeds. One wipes the stone. One sets out oranges, tea and flowers. Then everyone stands together and bows.
look.prompt: Why might a family share the work instead of one person doing it all?

check.q: What does the name Qingming mean?
check.why: Qingming means clear and bright; it is a spring festival in early April.

check.q: What do families do at graves on Qingming?
choices: Sweep, clean and bring food and flowers
Hang red paper on the door
check.why: On Qingming families clean ancestors' graves and set out food, tea and flowers.

check.q: Who are ancestors?
choices: Family members who lived long ago
check.why: Ancestors are family members from past generations, like great-grandparents.

lessons.title: Respect for Family
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught that caring for parents and honoring ancestors is an important part of being a good person.
reading: Why do families work so hard on Qingming? Part of the answer comes from Confucius. He was a teacher in China about 2,500 years ago. His students wrote down his words in a book called the Analects.

Confucius taught *xiao* (shyow). It means respect and care for your parents and family. In Analects, book 2, he says children should serve their parents with respect while they live. When parents die, children should bury them and honor them with proper rites.

Many families say Qingming puts this teaching into action. They remember who came before them. Not every family who keeps Qingming thinks of Confucius. For many, it is simply what their family has always done.

words.d: respect and care for parents and family; a key teaching of Confucius, often called filial piety
a teacher in China about 2,500 years ago whose sayings are in the Analects

look.title: Confucius on Parents
look.text: When parents are alive, serve them with respect. When they die, bury them with respect, and honor them with respect.
look.cite: Analects 2.5, retold in simple words from James Legge's translation, 1893
look.prompt: What three times does Confucius name? What should a child show at each one?

check.q: What does xiao mean?
choices: Respect and care for parents and family
check.why: Xiao is Confucius's teaching of respect and care for parents, often called filial piety.

check.q: Which book holds the sayings of Confucius?
check.why: Confucius's students wrote his sayings in the Analects.

check.q: Do all families who keep Qingming think about Confucius?
choices: No; for many it is simply family tradition
check.why: Many families keep Qingming as family custom without thinking of Confucius.

lessons.title: Dragon Boats and a Poet
lessons.mainIdea: The Dragon Boat Festival remembers the poet Qu Yuan with boat races and rice dumplings.
reading: Picture long, thin boats with dragon heads. Twenty rowers pull hard while a drummer beats the rhythm. This is the Dragon Boat Festival. It comes on the fifth day of the fifth month of the Chinese calendar, in early summer.

People tell that the festival remembers *Qu Yuan* (choo yuen). He was a poet and royal adviser who lived about 2,300 years ago. The story says he was sent away by his king, and he drowned himself in a river in sorrow for his land.

In the story, people raced out in boats to search for him. They threw rice into the water. Today people eat *zongzi*, sticky rice wrapped in leaves. Dragon boat races now take place around the world, including in Chicago.

words.d: a poet and adviser in ancient China remembered at the Dragon Boat Festival
sticky rice wrapped in leaves, eaten at the Dragon Boat Festival

look.title: Row Together
look.text: In a dragon boat, twenty rowers sit in pairs. A drummer at the front beats a steady rhythm. If each rower pulls whenever they want, the boat wobbles. When all pull on the beat, the boat flies.
look.prompt: What does a dragon boat race need from each rower? How is that like a family or a class?

check.q: Which person does the Dragon Boat Festival remember?
check.why: The festival is told as a way to remember the poet Qu Yuan.

check.q: What are zongzi?
check.why: Zongzi are sticky rice dumplings wrapped in leaves, eaten at the Dragon Boat Festival.

check.q: When is the Dragon Boat Festival?
choices: The first day of the first month
The fifth day of the fifth month
The fifteenth day of the eighth month
check.why: It falls on the fifth day of the fifth month of the Chinese calendar.

lessons.title: The Mid-Autumn Moon
lessons.mainIdea: At the Mid-Autumn Festival, families gather under the full moon to share mooncakes and hang lanterns.
reading: On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the moon is full and bright. This is the *Mid-Autumn Festival*. It comes in September or early October. Families gather outside to look at the moon together.

They share *mooncakes*. These are round pastries filled with sweet bean or lotus seed paste. Some have a salted egg yolk inside, like a small moon. Children carry lanterns shaped like rabbits, fish or stars.
The round moon and round cakes stand for a family that is whole and together. People who live far from home often say they look at the same moon as their family. It helps them feel close.

words.d: a fall festival on the full moon of the eighth month, with mooncakes and lanterns
a round pastry with a sweet filling, shared at the Mid-Autumn Festival

look.title: The Same Moon
look.text: A girl in Chicago eats a mooncake on her porch. Her grandfather in Guangzhou, China, sits on his balcony. It is not the same hour for both, but on the same festival night each one looks up at a full moon.
look.prompt: How could looking at the moon help family members who live far apart feel close?

check.q: When is the Mid-Autumn Festival?
choices: The first new moon of the year
The full moon of the eighth month
The fifth day of the fifth month
check.why: The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, at the full moon.

check.q: What do round mooncakes stand for?
choices: A family that is whole and together
check.why: Round cakes and the round moon stand for a family gathered together.

check.q: Which food is shared at the Mid-Autumn Festival?
check.why: Mooncakes belong to the Mid-Autumn Festival.

lessons.title: The Lady in the Moon
lessons.mainIdea: Families tell the old story of Chang'e, who floated up to live on the moon.
reading: At the Mid-Autumn Festival, grandparents often tell the story of *Chang'e* (chahng-uh). Long ago, the story says, ten suns burned the earth. A great archer named Hou Yi shot down nine of them and saved the people.

As a reward, Hou Yi was given a potion that would let him live forever. Chang'e drank it. Tellings differ on why. Some say she was protecting it from a thief. She floated up to the moon and lives there still, with a white rabbit.

There are many versions of this *legend*. Families tell the one they learned as children. Looking at the full moon, children try to spot the rabbit's shape. The story makes the moon feel like an old friend.

words.d: the lady in the moon in a Chinese legend told at the Mid-Autumn Festival
an old story passed down over many years, told in many versions

look.title: Two Tellings
look.text: Grandma's telling: Chang'e drank the potion to keep it from a thief, then floated to the moon. Uncle's telling: Chang'e drank it by mistake, and the moon became her quiet home. Both end with Chang'e and a white rabbit on the moon.
look.prompt: What is the same in both tellings? Why might a story have more than one version?

check.q: In the legend, who lives on the moon?
check.why: The Mid-Autumn legend says Chang'e lives on the moon with a white rabbit.

check.q: Who shot down nine suns in the story?
check.why: In the legend, the archer Hou Yi shot down nine of the ten suns.

check.q: Why do versions of the Chang'e story differ?
choices: Legends are passed down in many families and places
It was only written last year
check.why: A legend is told by many people over many years, so tellings differ.

lessons.title: Festivals Across Asia and America
lessons.mainIdea: Families in China, Taiwan, Korea, Vietnam and the United States keep these festivals in their own ways.
reading: Lunar New Year is not only Chinese. In Korea it is called *Seollal*. Families wear hanbok, bow to elders and eat rice cake soup. In Vietnam it is *Tet*. Families visit ancestors' altars and share sticky rice cakes.

The fall moon festival has many names too. In Korea, Chuseok is a harvest holiday when families visit graves and share food. In Vietnam, Tet Trung Thu is a children's festival with lanterns and lion dances.

Families brought these festivals to the United States. In Chicago's Chinatown, a Lunar New Year parade fills Wentworth Avenue. Each family mixes old ways and new ones. Two families may keep the same day very differently.

words.d: the Korean Lunar New Year, with bows to elders and rice cake soup
the Vietnamese Lunar New Year
a Korean fall harvest festival when families visit graves and share food

look.cite: Traditional Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese festival dates
look.prompt: Which festivals share the same month? How many months pass between the Dragon Boat and Mid-Autumn festivals?

check.q: What is Lunar New Year called in Vietnam?
check.why: Tet is the Vietnamese name for Lunar New Year.

check.q: Which is a Korean fall harvest festival?
check.why: Chuseok is the Korean fall harvest festival.

check.q: Where does Chicago's Lunar New Year parade take place?
check.why: Chicago's Chinatown holds its Lunar New Year parade along Wentworth Avenue.

review.q: Why do Chinese festival dates move on the everyday calendar?
review.why: Festivals follow the traditional lunisolar calendar, which counts months by the moon.

review.q: Which festival is a time to sweep ancestors' graves?
review.why: On Qingming, Tomb-Sweeping Day, families clean their ancestors' graves.

review.q: Which teaching of Confucius do many families link to Qingming?
choices: Xiao, respect for parents and family
review.why: Confucius taught xiao, care and respect for parents in life and after death.

choices: Zongzi and the Dragon Boat Festival
review.why: Zongzi, rice wrapped in leaves, belong to the Dragon Boat Festival.

review.q: Which story is told at the Mid-Autumn Festival?
review.why: The legend of Chang'e, the lady in the moon, belongs to the Mid-Autumn Festival.

choices: Twelve animals, one for each year
review.why: The Chinese zodiac is a cycle of twelve animals, one for each year.

review.q: Seollal and Tet are both names for which holiday?
review.why: Seollal (Korea) and Tet (Vietnam) are names for Lunar New Year.

review.q: What does the round moon stand for at Mid-Autumn?
choices: A family that is whole and together
review.why: Families say the round moon and round mooncakes stand for being together.
